lesson.title: Counting Waves: The Other Half of the Light Equation
lesson.summary: Frequency is the number of wave cycles that pass a fixed point every second, measured in hertz, and it is inversely related to wavelength through the speed of light, with higher frequency meaning higher photon energy.
lesson.body:
Wavelength measures a wave's length in space; frequency measures how often that wave repeats in time. Formally, frequency, given the symbol nu, is the number of complete wave cycles that pass a fixed point in exactly one second. Frequency is measured in hertz, abbreviated Hz, where one hertz equals one cycle per second. A radio station broadcasting at 100 megahertz is sending out electromagnetic waves that complete 100 million full cycles every single second.

Wavelength and frequency are not two independent properties; they are two views of the same wave, tied together by the fact that every electromagnetic wave travels at the same fixed speed in a vacuum, the speed of light, c, approximately 3.00 times 10 to the 8th meters per second. The relationship is c = lambda times nu, which rearranges to nu = c divided by lambda. Since c never changes for electromagnetic radiation, wavelength and frequency must always move in opposite directions: stretch out the wavelength and the frequency must drop, compress the wavelength and the frequency must rise. Long, lazy radio waves have low frequencies, often in the millions of hertz; the short, tight waves of gamma radiation have frequencies of billions of billions of hertz.

A worked calculation makes this concrete. Suppose you want the frequency of green light with a wavelength of 500 nanometers. First convert to meters, since c is in meters per second: 500 nanometers equals 500 times 10 to the negative 9th meters, or 5.00 times 10 to the negative 7th meters. Then apply nu = c / lambda: nu = (3.00 times 10 to the 8th meters per second) divided by (5.00 times 10 to the negative 7th meters), which works out to 6.00 times 10 to the 14th hertz. That is 600 trillion complete wave cycles passing any fixed point every second, which is a genuinely difficult number to picture intuitively, but the arithmetic itself is simple division once the units are consistent.

Frequency, not wavelength, is the quantity that plugs directly into the energy of a photon: E = h times nu, where h is Planck's constant, 6.626 times 10 to the negative 34th joule seconds. Because frequency sits directly in the numerator here, rather than in a denominator, the relationship with energy is a direct proportion rather than an inverse one: higher frequency light carries more energy per photon, full stop. This is the same conclusion wavelength led to (shorter wavelength means higher energy), arrived at from the other direction, since higher frequency and shorter wavelength always describe the identical wave.

This energy per photon, whether you calculate it from frequency or from wavelength, is what ultimately explains atomic line spectra and, by extension, why electron configurations matter for more than just bookkeeping. When an electron drops from a higher energy orbital to a lower energy orbital, the atom emits a photon whose energy exactly equals the energy gap between those two orbitals, and that photon's frequency, and equivalently its wavelength, is exactly what a spectroscope measures. The discrete, non continuous energy levels of orbitals are the reason atomic emission spectra show sharp individual lines of specific frequencies rather than a smooth rainbow, tying frequency and wavelength directly back to the quantized orbital structure this entire chapter sequence has been built around.
